rows.baseline_result: Plain `CREATE INDEX` acquires a `SHARE` lock on the table. This blocks all writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and other commands that take `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` or higher) for the duration of the index build, but it does **not** block reads (plain `SELECT`s proceed normally). Concurrent `SHARE` locks from other sessions are also fine, which is why multiple plain `CREATE INDEX` statements can technically coexist, but any table modification is locked out until the index build finishes. This is the reason `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` exists — it uses weaker locking to avoid blocking writes, at the cost of a slower, two-pass build.

rows.baseline_result:
No — the transaction will not start. Spring's `@Transactional` relies on a proxy wrapping the bean; self-invocation (`this.method()`) bypasses the proxy entirely, calling the raw method directly, so the AOP advice (and transaction interceptor) never runs.

To make it work: move the `@Transactional` method to a separate bean/service and call it through that injected bean, or inject the bean's own proxy (e.g., via `AopContext.currentProxy()` with exposed proxy enabled, or self-injection of the interface/bean) and call through it. Switching to AspectJ compile/load-time weaving instead of proxy-based AOP also avoids this limitation, since weaving modifies bytecode directly rather than relying on proxies.

rows.deep_consensus_result:
No. Spring's default proxy-based AOP only intercepts calls that go through the proxy object. When method A calls method B on 'this' (same bean instance), it's a plain Java call on the raw target object, not through the CGLIB/JDK proxy, so the @Transactional advice on B never fires (unless A itself already runs in a transaction, in which case B just joins it). No, this is unsafe. Trusting the token's own "alg" header lets an attacker choose the algorithm — e.g., switching RS256 to HS256 (confusing a public key for an HMAC secret) or to "none" to forge signatures, bypassing verification entirely (the classic "alg confusion" attack).

rows.deep_consensus_result:
No, it is not safe. If a verifier blindly trusts the "alg" value from the incoming JWT header, an attacker can forge tokens by choosing an algorithm that benefits them — classic attacks include setting "alg":"none" to skip signature verification entirely, or switching from an asymmetric algorithm (e.g., RS256) to a symmetric one (HS256) using the public key as the HMAC secret, since many libraries will happily verify an HS256 token against whatever key string they're given. It also recommends disallowing "none" and avoiding cross-algorithm confusion by keeping key types/algorithms strictly bound together.

rows.deep_consensus_result:

Its SQL grammar accepts SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED for standards compliance, but internally it is mapped to READ COMMITTED behavior. sprint4_original.ground_truth: Virtual threads should NEVER be pooled -- each should represent a task, using Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). They suit IO-bound work that spends most of its time blocked, not long-running CPU-intensive work.
sprint4_original.baseline_result:
No — don't pool virtual threads in a fixed-size (or any bounded) executor. Create a new one per task via `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`; they're cheap, unpooled, and meant to be discarded after use. Pooling them defeats their purpose and can cause artificial throughput limits/deadlocks under blocking loads.

They're best suited for IO-bound/blocking workloads (network calls, DB queries, file IO) with high concurrency, since blocking a virtual thread unmounts it from the carrier thread cheaply. For CPU-bound work, virtual threads offer no benefit over platform threads — use a fixed-size platform thread pool sized to CPU cores instead.
sprint4_original.deep_consensus_result:
No — virtual threads should not be placed in a fixed-size pool. They're cheap, lightweight, and designed to be created in huge numbers (often one per task/request) and discarded, so pooling defeats their purpose and can reintroduce the limited-concurrency problems platform-thread pools were meant to solve. Use Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() instead of a fixed pool. Virtual threads shine for IO-bound or blocking work (network calls, DB queries, file IO) because the JVM can unmount a blocked virtual thread from its carrier platform thread, freeing that carrier for other work. They offer no benefit for CPU-bound work — a blocked carrier isn't the bottleneck there, so traditional fixed-size thread pools sized to CPU cores remain the better fit for CPU-bound tasks.
